title: Cross-Partition Queries
description: Tackle scatter-gather latency, local vs global secondary indexes, denormalization as an escape hatch, and Vitess for cross-shard MySQL.

segments.text: You've partitioned your data beautifully. Every write goes to exactly one partition. Life is good. Then your product manager asks: 'Can we query all orders across all users for the last 24 hours?' Your single-partition dream just became a cross-partition nightmare. Let's talk about how to handle this without destroying your system.

Scatter-gather is the brute force approach. Send the query to every partition, collect results, merge them. With 100 partitions, you're making 100 parallel requests. The problem: your response time equals the slowest partition. Google's research showed that with 100 servers, if each has a one percent chance of a latency spike, you'll hit one on nearly every request.

This is the tail-at-scale problem. Even if each partition responds within 10 milliseconds at p99, querying 100 partitions means at least one will likely be slow. Your aggregate p99 becomes your per-partition p99.99. Hedged requests help: send the same query to a replica if the primary doesn't respond within a timeout, use whichever responds first.
segments.thought_prompt: If hedged requests double your query load, how would you decide when the latency improvement is worth the cost?

segments.text: Local secondary indexes live on the same partition as the data they index. Cassandra materialized views work this way. If you partition users by user_id and need to query by email, each partition maintains its own email-to-user index. The catch: querying by email still requires scatter-gather across all partitions to find the right one.

Global secondary indexes span all partitions. DynamoDB GSIs are a perfect example. The email-to-user index is itself partitioned, but by email hash. Now looking up a user by email hits exactly one index partition. But writes become more expensive: every user insert must also update the global index, potentially on a different node.

Sometimes the best answer is: don't query across partitions at all. Denormalize your data so that every query can be served by a single partition. Store the data in the shape your queries need. Yes, you're duplicating data. Yes, writes become more complex. But reads become trivially fast. This is the Cassandra philosophy: one table per query pattern.

Vitess, born at YouTube, solves cross-shard queries for MySQL. It sits between your application and multiple MySQL shards, making them look like one database. It parses SQL queries, routes single-shard queries directly, and handles cross-shard queries by scatter-gather with automatic result merging. Slack, HubSpot, and GitHub all run Vitess.

But Vitess can't magically fix physics. Cross-shard joins are still expensive. Cross-shard transactions use two-phase commit, adding latency. And aggregate queries across shards require the vtgate proxy to do the final merge in memory. Smart schema design that minimizes cross-shard operations is still your best friend, even with Vitess.
segments.thought_prompt: If cross-shard JOINs are expensive, how would you redesign a schema to avoid them?

segments.text: CQRS, Command Query Responsibility Segregation, is the architectural pattern here. Write to your partitioned primary store optimized for writes. Asynchronously project read-optimized views into Elasticsearch, Redis, or a read-only denormalized store. Queries hit the read store, never touching the partitioned write store. Eventual consistency is the price.

Cross-partition queries are the hidden cost of partitioning. Every partition boundary is a query boundary. The solutions trade complexity for performance: scatter-gather for simplicity, indexes for targeted queries, denormalization for speed, CQRS for separation. Know the cost of each, and choose based on your query patterns, not your comfort zone.
